title: Edinburgh to Glasgow
subtitle: Edinburgh → Glasgow, through the Trossachs
intro: Drive out of Edinburgh into the edge of the Highlands, spend a day on the water in the Trossachs, then roll down to Glasgow the scenic way — three days, filmed end to end.

dayGlance.title: The Highlands' Edge
dayGlance.sub: Mon — the Kelpies, Stirling Castle, then west to Callander.

dayGlance.title: The Water Day
dayGlance.sub: Tue — a cruise on Loch Katrine and the falls at Bracklinn.

dayGlance.title: The Bonnie Banks
dayGlance.sub: Wed — a slow day on Loch Lomond, then Glasgow after dark.

acts.label: Act 1 · The Highlands' edge
acts.tagline: Two giant horses, a castle that holds Scotland, then the mountains open up.
acts.narrative:
You leave Edinburgh and within the hour you're standing under two thirty-metre steel horses on the side of a canal, which is a strong way to start any film. The Kelpies are the biggest thing of their kind on Earth and named after a myth designed to frighten children away from water — the day's first 'wait, really?'

From there it climbs. Stirling Castle sits on a volcanic crag above the lowest crossing of the Forth, the pinch-point every army had to pass, which is why the old line runs 'hold Stirling, hold Scotland.' Wallace and Bruce both won the country back within sight of these walls. Give it the full two and a half hours.

Then the Lowlands run out. You drive west into Callander, the Victorian gateway to the Trossachs, drop your bags for two nights, and walk it off by the river as the light goes. Day one has carried you from a modern myth to a medieval one to the actual edge of the hills — and the camera has all three.

acts.label: Act 2 · The water day
acts.tagline: The nature day — a loch by steamer, a gorge on foot.
acts.narrative:
Day two is the quiet centre of the trip and the one that's all about water. You take a short, slow, single-track road to Loch Katrine — the loch that, thanks to one Walter Scott poem in 1810, kicked off the first tourism boom Scotland ever had. You cruise it on the water — the historic steamer SS Sir Walter Scott still runs the longer sailings — on a loch so protected (it supplies Glasgow's drinking water by gravity) that the boats have always run clean.

After lunch by the water you come back to Callander and walk up to Bracklinn Falls — fifteen minutes through the woods to a gorge, a run of falls, and a footbridge that's been rebuilt more than once since a flood tore the old one out in 2004. Keep it short or do the fuller loop; either way you get the sound of it on camera.

No big drives, no city — just the loch, the falls, and an easy last night in Callander before you drop down to Glasgow.

acts.label: Act 3 · The bonnie banks
acts.tagline: Loch Lomond all day, then Glasgow with its lights on — wind the trip down and sign off.
acts.narrative:
The last day slows right down. There's no dash for the city — you've all day on Loch Lomond and only need to be in Glasgow by nightfall. You start on the bonnie banks at Luss, a row of slate cottages on Britain's biggest stretch of fresh water, and take it slowly: the pier, the churchyard's thousand-year-old Viking stones, a long lunch by the water.

Then you drift south to the foot of the loch at Balloch — Loch Lomond Shores, the last paddle steamer in Britain moored at the pier, and a Victorian country park rolling down to the shore. It's the trip's final loch, and a gentle one; an easy afternoon before the tarmac takes over.

You reach Glasgow after six, as the light goes — which suits the 'dear green place.' The museums have shut, so tonight is the city with its lights on: dinner, the floodlit City Chambers on George Square, the traffic-coned Duke of Wellington, the murals of Merchant City, and a closing line down by the River Clyde. Stay central — there's a work meeting first thing on the 16th — and that's a wrap on Episode 03.

kelpies.name: The Kelpies
kelpies.story: The Kelpies are the biggest horse sculptures on the planet — thirty metres of steel each, the height of a ten-storey building, rearing up beside the canal at Helix Park. Sculptor Andy Scott modelled them on two real Clydesdales, Duke and Baron, the heavy working horses that once hauled barges along Scotland's canals. But the name is darker than the tribute: a kelpie is a shape-shifting water spirit from Scottish folklore, a horse that lures you onto its back and drags you down to drown. So you're standing under two monuments to a myth built to keep children away from the water. Wide lens, look up, let them fill the frame.
facts: The tallest equine sculptures in the world — 30 metres, around 300 tonnes of steel each
Named after the kelpie, a shape-shifting water-horse of legend that drowned its riders
Modelled on two real Clydesdales, Duke and Baron

walkPoints.name: The two heads
walkPoints.story: The two horses are deliberately different — Duke looking down mid-bow, Baron rearing to the sky — so together they read as one animal moving. Up close the stainless-steel skin catches the light like water.
walkPoints.todo: Shoot each head from directly below against the sky; the low angle is what sells the scale.

walkPoints.name: The canal basin
walkPoints.story: The Kelpies stand on an extension of the Forth & Clyde Canal — the very waterway the real Clydesdales once towed boats along. A short loop runs round the reflecting basin.
walkPoints.todo: Walk to the far side of the water for the mirror shot — both horses and their reflection in one frame.

walkPoints.name: Visitor Centre
walkPoints.story: Open daily, roughly 9:30–5. Coffee, the story of how they were built, and warmth if the wind is up off the canal.
walkPoints.todo: Grab the coffee; do a quick warm piece-to-camera inside if it's blowing a gale out there.

routeCard.trailingNote: Optional, 10 minutes away: the Falkirk Wheel — the world's only rotating boat lift. Free to walk up and watch it turn (only the boat trip is ticketed). Easy to pair with the Kelpies if you leave Edinburgh a little earlier.

stirling.name: Stirling Castle
stirling.story: There's an old line: whoever holds Stirling, holds Scotland. The castle sits on a plug of volcanic rock above the lowest bridging point of the River Forth — the pinch between Lowlands and Highlands — so for centuries every army heading north or south had to get past it. Two of the most famous battles in Scottish history were fought within sight of these walls: Stirling Bridge, where William Wallace wrecked an English army in 1297, and Bannockburn, where Robert the Bruce did it again in 1314. Inside, Mary Queen of Scots was crowned here as a nine-month-old baby, and James V built a Renaissance palace so show-off that the Great Hall was limewashed in gold. Give it two and a half hours; it earns them.
facts: "Hold Stirling, hold Scotland" — it guards the lowest crossing of the Forth
Mary Queen of Scots was crowned here aged nine months
Wallace's Stirling Bridge (1297) and Bruce's Bannockburn (1314) were both fought in sight of the walls

routeCard.sub: Old Town · top of the crag
routeCard.note: Park on the castle esplanade or below in the Old Town — the last stretch up is steep.
routeCard.walkLeadNote: These are all inside the one castle — a walk, not drives.

walkPoints.name: The Great Hall
walkPoints.story: The largest medieval banqueting hall in Scotland — and when they restored it they put back the original limewash, a bright golden ochre that horrified people used to grey ruins. It was meant to shout money and power. It does.
walkPoints.todo: Shoot the golden exterior harling for the colour, then the hammerbeam roof inside — the biggest of its kind in Scotland.

walkPoints.name: The Royal Palace
walkPoints.story: James V's Renaissance palace, built in the 1540s to impress a French wife. The ceiling of the King's Presence Chamber was studded with carved oak roundels — the Stirling Heads — faces of kings, nobles and jesters.
walkPoints.todo: Find the Stirling Heads (replicas on the ceiling, originals in the gallery). Slow pan across the carved faces.

walkPoints.name: The Chapel Royal
walkPoints.story: Rebuilt by James VI in 1594 in a hurry for his son's christening — the whole thing went up in about six months. This is roughly where the infant Mary was crowned Queen of Scots in 1543.
walkPoints.todo: Step inside for the painted frieze; it's a quiet beat between the big rooms.

walkPoints.name: The ramparts
walkPoints.story: From the walls you can see the Wallace Monument, the Ochil Hills, and the loops of the Forth where the battles were fought. On a clear day the whole gateway to the Highlands lays itself out.
walkPoints.todo: Walking piece-to-camera along the ramparts with the Wallace Monument over your shoulder.

routeCard.trailingNote: Optional, and pure vlog gold: Doune Castle is 8 miles on toward Callander, right on the A84. It's Castle Leoch in Outlander, Winterfell in the Game of Thrones pilot, and the castle from Monty Python and the Holy Grail. Adds ~45–60 min — trim Stirling or the Callander evening to fit.

see.name: The golden Great Hall
see.story: The biggest medieval hall in Scotland, limewashed back to its original shout-out-loud gold. Meant to intimidate; still does.
see.todo: Shoot the ochre exterior, then the huge hammerbeam roof inside.

see.name: James V's Renaissance Palace
see.story: A 1540s palace built to impress a French queen, its ceiling once studded with the carved-oak Stirling Heads.
see.todo: Pan slowly across the Stirling Heads — kings, nobles and jesters in wood.

see.name: The ramparts
see.story: From the walls you see the Wallace Monument and the Forth loops where Wallace and Bruce won Scotland back.
see.todo: Walking piece-to-camera with the Wallace Monument over your shoulder.

callander.name: Callander
callander.story: Callander is where the road runs out of Lowlands and the Highlands properly begin — the little town that's been the tourist gateway to the Trossachs since the Victorians. The River Teith runs through it, the main street is a row of stone shops and cafés, and it's your base for two nights. If it looks oddly familiar, it might be the telly: in the 1960s the BBC filmed Dr Finlay's Casebook here and turned Callander into the fictional town of Tannochbrae. Tonight is easy — no more driving. Walk the main street, down to the river, find dinner, and let the day settle.
facts: The Victorian gateway to the Trossachs and the Highlands
The River Teith runs right through the middle
It played the fictional town of Tannochbrae in the BBC's Dr Finlay's Casebook

loch-katrine.name: Loch Katrine
loch-katrine.angle: The loch that invented Scottish tourism
loch-katrine.story: Loch Katrine is the reason people started coming to the Highlands for fun. In 1810 Sir Walter Scott set his poem The Lady of the Lake right here, it became a runaway bestseller, and half of Victorian Britain suddenly wanted to see the Trossachs — the first tourism boom Scotland ever had. There's a quieter marvel too: since 1859 this loch has supplied Glasgow's drinking water, running twenty-six miles to the city entirely by gravity, no pumps — a piece of Victorian engineering still working today. Because it's Glasgow's protected water supply, the boats run clean — including the SS Sir Walter Scott, a steamer that's sailed this loch since 1900. The quick 45-minute round trip is on the modern launch; the steamer herself does the longer sailings, if you'd rather ride her. Either way, let the hills do the work.
facts: Sir Walter Scott's 1810 poem set here kicked off Scotland's first-ever tourism boom
It's supplied Glasgow's water since 1859 — 26 miles, entirely by gravity
The SS Sir Walter Scott steamer has sailed the loch since 1900

routeCard.note: About 9 miles from Callander on a narrow, winding A-road (not single-track) — allow 25–30 minutes; sat-nav struggles near the pier, so use the official coordinates. Book ahead. The quick 45-min circular runs roughly hourly (incl. ~11:00) on the modern launch; the historic steamer SS Sir Walter Scott sails at 10:30 (2hr) and 13:00 (1hr) if you'd rather ride her. Slide lunch and Bracklinn to match whichever you book.

walkPoints.name: Trossachs Pier
walkPoints.story: The jetty, a café, and a viewpoint looking down the loch. This is where Scott's tourists first stepped off the coach two hundred years ago.
walkPoints.todo: Get the establishing shot down the loch from the pier before you board.

walkPoints.name: The cruise
walkPoints.story: Forty-five minutes out and back on the water, the hills of the Trossachs rising on both sides. The quick circular at ~11:00 runs on the modern launch; the historic steamer SS Sir Walter Scott does the longer sailings if you'd rather ride her.
walkPoints.todo: Shoot wide from the deck, keep the horizon level, mind the wind on the mic. Grab a piece-to-camera with the wake behind you.

walkPoints.name: Lunch by the water
walkPoints.story: Back at the pier there's food and a bench with a loch view — an easy break before Bracklinn.
walkPoints.todo: Slow B-roll of the loch, then eat.

routeCard.trailingNote: Optional, if you want a hill and a view: Ben A'an sits right on this road at Loch Achray — a short, steep 1.5–2.5 hr climb to arguably the best view in the Trossachs. Slot it before or after the cruise.

see.story: Café, viewpoint and the jetty where Scott's Victorian tourists first arrived.
see.todo: Establishing shot down the loch before you board.

see.story: A 45-min round trip on the modern launch (the historic SS Sir Walter Scott, sailing since 1900, does the longer runs), on a loch that waters Glasgow by gravity.

bracklinn.name: Bracklinn Falls
bracklinn.story: Just above Callander, the Keltie Water throws itself through a rocky gorge in a run of falls called Bracklinn — a fifteen-minute walk through the woods from the car park. The Victorians put it on the map — the old iron bridge here was said to be built for a visit by Queen Victoria. The bridge is its own small drama: the footbridge was ripped out by a flood in 2004, an award-winning timber span went up in 2010 but wore out, and the one you cross now is a sturdy metal bridge from 2023. You can keep it short — walk to the main viewpoint and back — or, if it's dry and you've got the legs, do the fuller loop. You don't need boots, but you do need closed shoes with grip.
facts: A run of waterfalls on the Keltie Water in a rocky gorge above Callander
The 2004 flood destroyed the footbridge; today's metal span (2023) is the latest to cross the gorge
The Victorians made it famous — the old iron bridge was said to be built for a Queen Victoria visit

routeCard.note: Closed shoes with grippy soles — the path is rooty and can be slick. Not full boots, just not worn-out trainers.

walkPoints.name: The woodland path
walkPoints.story: A short trail through birch and oak from the car park down towards the sound of water — you hear the falls before you see them.
walkPoints.todo: B-roll of the light through the trees on the way in; it sets up the reveal.

walkPoints.name: The gorge bridge
walkPoints.story: The footbridge over the gorge at the falls' loudest point — the latest of several here, a metal span from 2023 that replaced an award-winning timber bridge worn out by the weather.
walkPoints.todo: Shoot the bridge from the bank, then from on it looking down into the gorge — mind your footing.

walkPoints.name: The falls & viewpoint
walkPoints.story: The Keltie Water drops through a series of ledges into a dark pool — more power than height, and loud after rain.
walkPoints.todo: Main viewpoint for the hero shot. Piece-to-camera with the falls behind you; you'll have to talk up over the noise.

see.todo: B-roll of light through the trees on the way in.

see.name: The gorge bridge
see.story: The current metal footbridge (2023) over the gorge — the latest of several since the 2004 flood.
see.todo: Shoot it from the bank, then from on it looking into the gorge.

see.name: The falls
see.story: The Keltie Water drops through dark ledges — more power than height, loud after rain.
see.todo: Hero shot from the viewpoint; piece-to-camera over the noise.

luss.name: Luss & Loch Lomond
luss.story: Luss is the picture-postcard village on the west shore of Loch Lomond — a neat row of slate-and-sandstone cottages that were actually built as workers' housing for the local slate quarries in the 1800s, then quietly became one of the prettiest villages in Scotland. The loch behind them is the biggest stretch of fresh water in Britain by area. This is the 'bonnie banks o' Loch Lomond' of the song — and the cheerful tune hides a grim story: 'ye'll tak' the high road and I'll tak' the low road' is said to be a captured Jacobite soldier telling his friend that he'll get home first, because the 'low road' is the road of the dead. Like Callander, Luss has a TV past too — it was the village of Glendarroch in the soap Take the High Road for over twenty years. Last nature stop before the city: no hiking, no rush.
facts: Loch Lomond is the largest area of fresh water in Britain
The cottages were built for slate-quarry workers, not for the postcards
The "low road" in the Loch Lomond song is said to mean the road of the dead

walkPoints.name: The slate cottages
walkPoints.story: The famous row of low cottages, built around 1800 for the men working the Luss slate quarries up the hill. The slate roofs are local; the roses out front came much later, for the tourists.
walkPoints.todo: Walk the lane slowly for a tracking shot; the cottages line up like a set.

walkPoints.name: The pier & shore
walkPoints.story: A short stone pier reaches out into Loch Lomond — the classic bonnie-banks view, islands scattered down the water.
walkPoints.todo: Walk to the end of the pier for the wide loch shot; get the islands in frame.

walkPoints.name: Luss Parish Church
walkPoints.story: In the churchyard is a hogback stone — an 11th-century Anglo-Scandinavian grave-marker, from when Norse settlers were here on the loch.
walkPoints.todo: Find the hogback stone by the church — worn, whale-backed, easy to walk past.

walkPoints.name: Coffee with a view
walkPoints.story: A café or two by the shore for a last Highland coffee before Glasgow.
walkPoints.todo: Quick warm piece-to-camera — the last nature beat of the trip.

see.name: The slate cottages
see.story: Built around 1800 for slate-quarry workers, now one of Scotland's prettiest rows.
see.todo: Slow tracking shot down the lane — they line up like a set.

see.name: The pier & bonnie banks
see.story: A stone pier into Loch Lomond, Britain's largest stretch of fresh water, islands down the loch.
see.todo: Walk to the pier's end for the wide shot with the islands.

see.name: A Viking hogback stone
see.story: An 11th-century Anglo-Scandinavian grave-marker sits in the parish churchyard.
see.todo: Find the whale-backed stone by the church — easy to miss.

see.story: No rush today — this is the day's main event now, not a quick stop.
see.todo: Take a proper lunch by the water before drifting south to Balloch.

balloch.name: Balloch & Loch Lomond Shores
balloch.story: Balloch sits at the southern tip of Loch Lomond, where the loch narrows and pours out into the River Leven — the busy, easygoing foot of the loch after Luss's postcard calm. This is the family end: Loch Lomond Shores, a waterfront of shops and cafés with the Maid of the Loch, Britain's last paddle steamer, moored at the pier; and Balloch Castle Country Park, two hundred acres of Victorian parkland and gardens rolling down to the water, a castle of 1808 at the top. It's an easy, unhurried afternoon on the way south — stretch your legs by the water, grab a coffee or a loch cruise, and let the trip wind down before the city. Last loch of the trip.
facts: The foot of Loch Lomond, where it drains into the River Leven
The Maid of the Loch — Britain's last paddle steamer — is moored at Loch Lomond Shores
Balloch Castle Country Park runs 200 acres of gardens down to the water

walkPoints.story: The waterfront complex at the foot of the loch — shops, cafés, an aquarium, and boat trips out onto the water. Moored at the pier is the Maid of the Loch, the last paddle steamer built in Britain, slowly being restored.
walkPoints.todo: Get the Maid of the Loch at the pier and a wide of the loch opening out to the north.

walkPoints.name: Balloch Castle Country Park
walkPoints.story: Two hundred acres of Victorian parkland sloping down to the loch, with a castle of 1808 at the top and walled gardens below. Free to wander.
walkPoints.todo: Walk down to the shoreline for the last loch B-roll; the lawns frame the water nicely.

glasgow.name: Glasgow
glasgow.angle: The dear green place, after dark
glasgow.story: Glasgow is the finish line, and you're arriving as the light goes — which suits it. The museums have shut, so tonight isn't about galleries; it's the city in the evening. The name is fondly translated as 'dear green place,' but modern Glasgow is Victorian sandstone and swagger: George Square and the City Chambers, an 1888 pile with a marble-and-gold interior, built when the Clyde shipyards were launching a fifth of the world's ships; the Duke of Wellington outside the Gallery of Modern Art, wearing the traffic cone Glaswegians have kept on his head for forty years because the council finally gave up removing it; the mural trail brightening the lanes of Merchant City. Eat well, walk it off through the centre, and take your closing line down to the River Clyde at night. That's a wrap on Episode 03.
facts: Glasgow's name means "dear green place" (Gaelic Glaschu)
The Duke of Wellington statue has worn a traffic cone for 40 years — the council gave up removing it
The Clyde shipyards once built around a fifth of all the world's ships

routeCard.sub: Evening in the city · arrive ~6:15 PM · ~2h, unhurried
routeCard.note: Museums are shut by now, so this is a walking evening — park central near your room and go on foot; the centre is compact. Best base for dinner is Merchant City (steps from the murals and George Square). Two July heads-ups: mid-July sunset is ~9:50 PM, so you're mostly in daylight and dusk — lean into golden hour, the true floodlit look only comes near closing; and George Square is finishing a £20m revamp, so its south side may still be fenced on 15 July (the City Chambers and the Wellington cone are unaffected).
routeCard.walkLeadNote: Arrive ~6:15 and check in, then keep it easy: dinner, then one short floodlit loop — George Square down to the Clyde is about an hour on foot, everything a few minutes apart. It's the wind-down, so stop when you're done; there's a meeting in the morning.

walkPoints.name: Dinner — West End or Merchant City
walkPoints.story: Two good options: the West End around Byres Road (lively, studenty, endless choice) or Merchant City in the centre (grander, and right by the night walk). Either works.
walkPoints.todo: Eat first — you've earned it. Keep any to-camera short and warm.

walkPoints.name: George Square — Chambers & the cone
walkPoints.story: The civic heart: the City Chambers, an over-the-top Victorian pile (opened 1888) with a marble-and-gold interior, built at the height of Glasgow's shipbuilding wealth — and two minutes round the corner at the Gallery of Modern Art, the Duke of Wellington under the traffic cone Glaswegians won't let the council remove.
walkPoints.todo: Two shots, same square: the lit-up City Chambers façade, and the Wellington cone — the city in one frame.

walkPoints.name: The River Clyde at night
walkPoints.story: A ten-minute walk down through Merchant City's mural-painted lanes brings you to the river that built Glasgow — quiet and lit at night, the water that once launched a fifth of the world's ships.
walkPoints.todo: Grab a mural on the way down, then your closing sign-off by the Clyde — last line of Episode 03.

see.todo: Eat first (~1h); keep to-camera short and warm.
